articles.title: What’s behind the US deal to seize control of Venezuelan oil reserves?
articles.summary: Few details have emerged about deal between Washington and Caracas, criticised as takeover of Venezuela’s resources.
articles.body:
The United States has announced that it has secured control of a substantial portion of Venezuela’s vast oil reserves, after President Donald Trump pledged to “take back” the South American country’s energy resources.

On Friday, Trump announced that his government and that of Venezuela’s interim President Delcy Rodriguez had reached a deal to give the US majority control over more than 65 billion barrels’ worth of proven oil reserves.

Details remain unclear. But the deal will involve 17 strategic oil fields in Venezuela. The US government has said it will partner with a private business to extract the fuel.

“The United States of America has just entered into an Agreement with the Country of Venezuela on, THE BIGGEST OIL DEAL IN WORLD HISTORY!” Trump wrote in a social media post celebrating the announcement.

What has been said so far, and what could the new deal mean for US-Venezuela relations? We answer those questions and more in this explainer.

The deal reportedly involves 65 billion barrels of Venezuelan oil reserves.

That amounts to roughly a fifth of Venezuela’s proven oil reserves. As of 2023, the US government estimates that Venezuela has 303 billion barrels of oil reserves, the largest known deposit in the world.

Approximately 17 percent of the world’s oil supply is estimated to be in the South American country.

But some analysts have questioned the 65-billion-barrel total Trump announced. With no fixed terms released, there has been speculation that Trump may have made a splashy announcement to help jumpstart the US economy.

“The 65 billion barrel number is a red herring and will have little relevance to any actual deals — the real relevant details of which are still almost entirely unknown,” oil market researcher Rory Johnston said in a social media post.

“It’s just a classic big number that Trump was sure to jump all over and will repeat ad nauseam going forward.”

Trump has said that the deal “MORE THAN DOUBLES American Oil Reserves”.

Government estimates indicate that proven US oil reserves are declining, standing at approximately 46 billion barrels by the end of 2024.

The US government also operates a Strategic Petroleum Reserve, an emergency supply of oil to help ensure steady domestic supplies.

But the emergency stockpile is shrinking, with only 289.7 million barrels in storage facilities designed to hold up to 714 million barrels. Trump has indicated that Friday’s deal will help restore the US oil reserves, which have hit their lowest levels since 1982.

The year 2026 has seen dramatic changes for Venezuela and its relationship with the US.

Since 2013, the South American country had been led by socialist President Nicolas Maduro, whose tenure had been defined by a series of disputed elections and crackdowns on political dissent.

Trump and Maduro had repeatedly clashed, with Trump accusing the Venezuelan leader of sending drug-traffickers into the US, and Maduro accusing Trump of foreign interference in domestic politics.

Their conflict came to a head on January 3. For weeks, US military vessels had been amassing off the shore of Venezuela, and during the early morning hours, Trump authorised an operation to abduct and imprison the Venezuelan leader.

Maduro now awaits trial on drug- and weapons-related charges in New York.

In the aftermath of the attack, Trump backed Maduro’s former vice president, Rodriguez, to lead the government in Caracas. She was sworn in shortly afterwards.

The Trump administration also announced that Washington would take control of Venezuela’s oil exports “indefinitely”.

Critics have pointed out that the Trump administration has pressured Rodriguez to comply with its demands. “If she doesn’t do what’s right, she is going to pay a very big price, probably bigger than Maduro,” Trump told The Atlantic magazine in January.

What are Trump’s claims to Venezuela’s oil?

Experts have denounced US intervention in Venezuela as illegal under international law.

But the Trump administration has made the claim to Venezuelan oil resources a key pillar in its involvement in the South American country.

In the lead-up to the January 3 attack, Trump and his allies advanced an argument that Venezuela’s oil supplies belonged to the US, due to a history of early fuel exploration in the country.

They also denounced the Venezuelan government’s efforts to expropriate oil resources from private companies, as part of an effort to nationalise the fossil fuel industry.

In December, Trump announced a blockade around Venezuela to prevent the sale of oil, its largest export. As justification, he accused Venezuela of having “stolen oil fields” from the US.

His adviser, Stephen Miller, separately called the nationalisation of Venezuela’s oil industry “the largest recorded theft of American wealth and property”.

International law, however, gives countries “permanent sovereignty” over their resources, to protect them from unwanted foreign exploitation.

Friday marked the six-month anniversary of the US-Israel war on Iran .

Once the war began on February 28, Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz to commercial traffic. Nearly one-fifth of the world’s oil and natural gas supply passed freely through the strait before the war.

The shutdown has resulted in a spike in global oil prices, including in the US, where voters will head to the polls in November for midterm elections.

The American Automobile Association (AAA) announced this week that it expects this month to be the most expensive August on record for petrol prices, with US consumers paying an average of more than $4 a gallon (3.8 litres).

The dispute over the strategic waterway is ongoing, as is the war itself. Ongoing military actions have also strained US oil supplies.

How is the Trump administration framing the new oil deal?

Trump has repeatedly held up Venezuela, under Rodriguez’s leadership, as a model for how it would like to deal with foreign adversaries like Iran.

He has also touted Washington’s control over Venezuelan oil supplies as a boon for the US economy during the midterm election period.

“We’re doing great in Venezuela. We’re taking a lot of oil from Venezuela, and we’re getting along great with them,” Trump told supporters at a rally in Las Vegas this month.

He then claimed to have “paid for the war” against Venezuela “with what we’ve taken out” from the country.

“That’s the old-fashioned way, right? The old-fashioned way,” Trump told the crowd. “To the victor belong the spoils, right?”

In announcing Friday’s deal, Trump pledged that the resulting increase in the US oil supply “will substantially lower Gas Prices for all Americans”. The cost of living is expected to be a key issue in this year’s midterm races.

Separately, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, a foreign policy hawk, framed the oil deal as a victory for Trump’s America First platform.

“It demonstrates how President Trump’s bold foreign policy is driving America First wins: securing stable reserves and low-cost oil in our Hemisphere and lowering gas prices here at home,” Rubio wrote .

He also asserted the deal would be mutually beneficial to Venezuela. The agreement, he said, will increase the private investment needed for “the reconstruction of Venezuela’s economy”.

How has Delcy Rodriguez responded to the deal?

Rodriguez has likewise presented the deal as a win for her administration.

In a message on the social media platform Telegram, she called the agreement “historic” and said that it would have “a significant impact on our nation’s revival”.

“It will facilitate a significant flow of investment aimed at the recovery and reconstruction of strategic infrastructure for the development of our hydrocarbons industry,” Rodriguez wrote.

Venezuela has long struggled with an economic crisis that has caused shortages of basic supplies and spiralling inflation. Nearly 8 million Venezuelans have left the country since 2014 due to political repression and economic concerns.

Critics have pointed to government corruption and mismanagement of state industries, including the oil and mining sectors, as one of the reasons for the economic decline. Another commonly cited reason is the impact of heavy US sanctions on the Venezuelan economy.

Since taking office as interim president, however, Rodriguez has led a campaign to increase private investment in Venezuela’s industries, at the behest of the Trump administration.

Her government has estimated that Friday’s deal will net $209bn in taxes for Venezuela, plus $100bn in investments.

Media reports indicate that the Rodriguez government has given the Trump administration the right to use the oil reserves for 100 years.

Washington has a long record of intervention in Latin America, and Trump has sought to assert US dominance over the Western Hemisphere as part of a policy he calls the “Donroe Doctrine”.

Critics have depicted Friday’s arrangement as a bid to seize Venezuela’s resources, akin to what Western powers did during colonial times.

Shortly before the deal was announced, energy analyst Gregory Brew likened reports of the impending agreement to oil concessions sought by the British Empire in the early 20th century.

“Such a thing is without precedent,” Brew wrote on social media. “The closest thing would be BP [British Petroleum] (back when it was majority owned by the UK govt) claiming ownership of Iraqi and Iranian oil reserves pre-WWII.”

Trump himself has embraced the colonial-era slogan “Manifest Destiny”, as part of his plan for a “growing nation” that “increases our wealth” and “expands our territory”.

Could the Venezuela model be applied elsewhere?

Trump has floated the possibility of claiming oil reserves in other parts of the world, too.

In 2011, long before he made his first successful bid for public office, Trump suggested that the US should use its military power to extract oil from other countries.

“I would take the oil,” Trump said of the US military intervention in Libya. That same year, he repeated the remark in reference to the US occupation of Iraq.

During his second term as president, Trump has voiced similar intentions towards Iran. In April, he posted on social media, “With a little more time, we can easily OPEN THE HORMUZ STRAIT, TAKE THE OIL, & MAKE A FORTUNE.” He has also proposed making the Strait of Hormuz a US territory.

articles.title: Four baby goats at mobile petting zoo in North Carolina test positive for rabies
articles.summary: Four baby goats from a North Carolina mobile petting zoo tested positive for rabies and were euthanized, and health officials are asking anyone who may have had contact with them to reach out for possible treatment.
articles.body: Four baby goats from a North Carolina mobile petting zoo tested positive for rabies and were euthanized, and health officials are asking anyone who may have had contact with them to reach out for possible treatment. The North Carolina Department of Health and Human Services said anyone who had contact with the baby goats at Farm Adventures’ location in Harmony, North Carolina, or at one of its mobile events between July 28 and Thursday should contact local health officials. “The petting zoo held off-site events involving children and elderly individuals across multiple counties within that time frame,” the department said. Health professionals may determine whether people who had contact with the baby goats need further examination or precautionary medication, it said. Without it, rabies is almost always fatal in humans, the state health department said. Farm Adventures said in a statement posted to Facebook that it is monitoring its other animals for signs of the viral disease. “The affected animals, our four precious baby goats, have been euthanized to prevent further spread,” it said. The baby goats were too young for vaccination and were bitten by a skunk that was found in their separate pen, the petting zoo said. It said it was unaware the goats had been bitten, and that they did not show typical symptoms of the disease. After the first goat’s death, the petting zoo sent its body to be tested, it said. It was unclear when the skunk was found in the pen. Skunks are one of the animals most often found with rabies, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. People can get rabies through pets, wild animals and other humans through a bite, a scratch or even infected saliva, it said. It can take weeks after exposure for early symptoms to begin, including flulike illness, feeling weak, fevers, headaches and a prickling or itching sensation, health officials say. North Carolina hasn’t had a reported human case since 2011, the state health department said. Roughly 100,000 Americans a year receive a rabies vaccine following a potential exposure, according to the CDC. It characterizes rabies as “a rare but serious public health concern.” The petting zoo said it’s cooperating with state and local government officials. “We are working closely with public health officials, the North Carolina Department of Agriculture, and animal control to address this issue and ensure the safety of our animals and clients,” it said in its statement. The petting zoo, responding to a comment on Facebook, said it’s hoping its customers are unaffected. “I am truly concerned about anyone that has been able to enjoy our animals,” the comment said. “We would NEVER intend to put anyone in danger.” NBC News has reached out to the petting zoo for additional comment.

articles.title: Everest veterans, mountain guides enter choked hydropower tunnel to rescue 6
articles.summary: South Asia News: TRISHULI BAZAAR (NUWAKOT, NEPAL): Everest veterans and some of Nepal's most highly trained mountain guides joined rescue operations in flood-ravaged R.
articles.body: TRISHULI BAZAAR (NUWAKOT, NEPAL): Everest veterans and some of Nepal's most highly trained mountain guides joined rescue operations in flood-ravaged Rasuwa, with a specialist team entering a mud-choked hydropower tunnel Saturday and pushing around 120m inside before thick sludge and debris blocked further movement. The deployment brought skills normally used on Himalayan expeditions - rope fixing, cliff access, helicopter longline operations and movement through unstable terrain - into parts of the disaster zone where roads had disappeared and conventional rescue methods were proving difficult.The team entered the tunnel at Chilime hydropower project, where six people were believed to be inside. IFMGA-certified guide Ashish Gurung, Dorjee Sherpa and veteran climber Jenjen Lama moved into the tunnel using rope protection and fixed lines before chest-deep sludge stopped them. They recovered a camera bag during the search and concluded that pumps and excavation equipment would be needed before rescuers could safely move deeper.The Chilime search formed part of a much larger tunnel rescue challenge across the flood-hit hydropower corridor. Six people were believed trapped inside the Chilime tunnel, while at Upper Trishuli-1 around 300 workers were believed to remain inside its tunnel system.The affected workforce across the projects included Nepalese, Indian, Chinese and South Korean nationals, with authorities still reconciling project attendance records and rescue lists to establish exactly how many remained trapped or uncontactable.Lama, a veteran high-altitude guide, has summited Mount Everest six times and Ama Dablam 12 times, besides climbing Lhotse and Manaslu. Another climber in the wider operation was Dawa Jangbu Sherpa, a guide with more than two decades of mountaineering experience.The specialist contingent also included Dawa Singhi Hyolmo, an IFMGA-certified international mountain guide and national mountaineering instructor with more than a decade of high-altitude experience, and fellow IFMGA-certified guides Man Raj Gurung and Ashish Gurung. Pemba Wangchu Sherpa, Bikram Karki, Sabin Thakuri, Geshman Tamang, Sandesh Sherpa and Chhiring Sherpa were among other trained climbers and rescuers mobilised.NNMGA and Nepal Mountaineering Instructors Association deployed helicopter longline and ground teams after floods swept away roads and bridges and left parts of Rasuwa accessible only across steep slopes, cliffs and unstable ground.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Russian strike on a Ukrainian warehouse kills 37 in the war’s deadliest attack this year
articles.summary: A Russian drone struck a warehouse west of Kyiv that Ukrainian officials say was storing shells, mines and other ammunition, sparking massive explosions and fires that swept through dozens of nearby homes and buildings and killing 37 people.
articles.body: MYLA, Ukraine — A Russian drone struck a warehouse west of Kyiv that Ukrainian officials say was storing shells, mines and other ammunition, sparking massive explosions and fires that swept through dozens of nearby homes and buildings and killing 37 people. The Friday night attack on the warehouse in Myla, a village in the Bucha district, was the war’s deadliest attack this year and came on the second of three days of nearly round-the-clock Russian strikes that have severely disrupted life in and around the Ukrainian capital. Attacks on the capital and, to a lesser extent, the rest of Ukraine have been nearly constant since Thursday. Kyiv officials say Russia builds up missile stocks and launches major attacks every few days, hoping to exhaust Ukrainian defenses through the sheer weight of numbers. The warehouse strike sparked fires that raced through homes and damaged at least 50 residential buildings, said Tymur Tkachenko, who heads the local regional military administration. He was later cited by local media as saying 34 of the people killed were residents of a care home for elderly and disabled people. More than 370 people were evacuated. The blasts rocked Myla, causing people to frantically seek cover. “At about 8 p.m., the drone hit a warehouse somewhere and then the detonation began,” Oleksandr Vodolaz, a village resident, told The Associated Press. “No one knew that weapons were stored there.” As crews raced to get people to safety and extinguish blazes, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described the attack as a “terrible situation” and said it appeared to be the result of “terrible negligence on the part of those who stored explosives right next to people.” He noted that Ukrainian law forbids the storage of ammunition close to people’s homes and said criminal proceedings had been opened. “Those who allowed this to happen must be held accountable for their decisions,” the president said. Kyiv investigates warehouse targeted in attack In a social media post Saturday, Zelenskyy shed more light on the situation. “The first strike was on an ammunition storage site that definitely shouldn’t have been there – a Defense Forces storage facility. Shells, mines, other ammunition, and drones detonated.” Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi didn’t specify what was in the warehouse, but he referenced a July attack on the Kyiv suburb of Vyshneve that struck an ammunition depot, killing 22 people and triggering detonations and fires that tore through nearby homes. “Unfortunately, we can already see that the terrible tragedy in Vyshneve did not become a lesson,” Koretskyi said. “In the fifth year of a full-scale invasion, making the same mistakes is criminal negligence. And all those guilty, without exception, must be severely punished so that such situations do not happen again.” The 37 killed surpassed the 31 who died in a July 2 strike on Kyiv, which had been the war’s deadliest attack of 2026. Russia’s Defense Ministry said it hit a warehouse in Myla that was storing components and launch boosters for long-range drones. It also said it attacked the ports of Mykolaiv and Izmail, and a logistics center and warehouse facilities storing parts for Ukraine’s Flamingo cruise missiles in the Kyiv region. Russian jet-powered drones pose a problem for Kyiv Russian strikes damaged homes and apartment blocks in the southern Kherson region on Saturday, killing two people and wounding 27 more, including a child, Oleksandr Prokudin, head of the region administration, said in a statement. Prokudin said earlier in the week that Russia had intensified its attacks on critical infrastructure in the region, which is about 70% under Russian control. He also urged tens of thousands of residents to move to safer regions because of the possibility of prolonged power and heating outages this winter. Although officials haven’t said whether they were used in the warehouse attack, Russia has significantly increased its use of jet-powered drones, and their numbers will keep growing as Moscow sees their effectiveness, Pavlo Palisa, deputy head of Ukraine’s presidential office, told reporters Friday. “Means of attack always outpace means of defense. We will certainly need to adapt. It will take time,” Palisa said. He said interceptor drones currently available to Ukraine, which could theoretically intercept jet-powered drones, have not yet demonstrated the expected effectiveness, though Ukraine is working on solutions. Ukraine vows to increase long-range strikes Meanwhile, Ukraine has stepped up its long-range attacks on Russian military industries and energy facilities in recent months. The attacks, which use domestically made drones, are meant to cut into a source of Moscow’s war funding and make Russians feel the consequences. In his evening statement to the nation Friday, Zelenskyy said Kyiv hoped to increase its long-range strikes to reach 1000 drone launches every day. “Right now, we average over 300 of our long-range sanctions,” Zelenskyy said, his preferred term for Kyiv’s long-range attacks that have also lately targeted Russian large-scale online retailers. “There must be more. We have a very specific goal, and we will achieve it.” Moscow’s forces destroyed 313 Ukrainian drones overnight, Russia’s Defense Ministry said Saturday. Ukrainian drone attacks wounded 11 people in Russia’s Rostov region, Gov. Yuri Slyusar said. Writing on social media, he said that nine people were hospitalized, including four children.

articles.title: Our DNA dilemma: Why we broke the law to make sure we were not siblings
articles.summary: A French couple - both conceived by sperm donors - wanted children. But with home DNA tests illegal, how could they be sure they were not related?
articles.body:
For years, Arthur Kermalvezen, the child of a sperm donor, saw possible fathers everywhere he went. "I imagined it might be my teacher, the people I saw on the bus... and I was very angry because it's impossible to live like this."

When, as an adult, he fell in love with Audrey, another sperm donor baby from Paris, the question became even more pressing.

Audrey describes the moment they met at a gathering for donor conceived activists in 2010 as "love at first sight" - but was this connection a romantic or genetic attraction?

When they were born, there were only two sperm banks in Paris and many men had made multiple donations - so there was a real possibility they could be half-siblings.

Before building a life together, Arthur and Audrey needed to know whether they were related. But in France, laws governing genetic testing and donor anonymity made finding the answer extremely difficult.

In France, only a research scientist, doctor or judge can order and supervise a genetic test, and people can be fined more than €3,500 ($4,288; £3,191) for possessing a home testing kit. As a result, companies such as 23andMe, Ancestry and MyHeritage don't make their kits available in France.

Supporters of the law, in place since 1994, say it stops sensitive genetic data being given to commercial companies, and prevents family disputes being caused by unexpected results.

But Arthur points out that France is the only country in Europe that criminalises the use of such tests.

Even before her parents told her as an adult that she was donor-conceived, Audrey had qualified as a lawyer, specialising in bioethics law. Because of this, she fully understood that French law had guaranteed donor anonymity, even after a donor's death.

But Audrey had been conceived in 1979, before any such legislation existed.

While searching for other donor-conceived people born before 1994, Audrey came across Arthur. He had written a book detailing his desire to learn more about his biological origins.

Audrey says she was struck by how precisely he expressed feelings she herself had struggled to articulate. Both had loving families, yet both found themselves drawn to questions about the unknown people who had helped to create them.

When they met in person the chemistry was immediate. So was the problem.

Before they could move from platonic friendship to a romantic relationship, and even build a life together, they had to know the truth about their fathers. But no one in authority was willing to tell them.

After months of searching, they found a doctor in southern France who, for €900 ($1,028; £764) in cash, conducted a genetic test which found that they were not related. But their unease remained as the doctor was breaking the law in sharing that result with them.

"We were worried he was a charlatan," Audrey says.

They considered using a home-testing kit to confirm the result, but as a lawyer, Audrey was determined to act within the law.

So, from 2010, she launched a series of legal challenges to the French system.

She wanted to know whether her donor was still alive and, if so, whether he still wished to remain anonymous. Could she access non-identifying information about how many times he had donated and whether Arthur could be among her half-siblings?

After three years of legal challenges, the couple took a 'leap of faith' and got married.

In 2015, France's highest administrative court rejected Audrey's final appeal.

Shortly before the birth of their first child, a doctor agreed to investigate what information might exist about their respective donors. Under French law, a medical practitioner has access to this information about their patients, but is not allowed to share it with them.

The doctor found that their donors were born in different years - and so could not be the same man. A life-changing piece of information, but one they only gained because a doctor agreed to break the rules.

"It's completely weird," Audrey says, "because it means that the doctor can know more than me... about me."

Even with this new information, Arthur still worried they could be related, so after years of resisting it, they finally took a home DNA test.

Campaigners say the French ban has done little to stop people taking home tests, with the advocacy group DNA Pass estimating that well over a million French people have taken one. Many order them via friends in countries where they are legally obtainable - or by using forwarding services in neighbouring countries.

The DNA results soon opened more doors. After 30 years of imagining who his father might be, Arthur finally made contact with his sperm donor on Christmas Day in 2017.

But Audrey had the greatest shock. Among her DNA matches was a woman named Sophie whom she'd represented in court. The two women had been fighting for similar legal rights.

"I discovered that Sophie - a woman whose case I had pleaded in court - was my biological sister," Audrey says.

Audrey and Arthur had taken their DNA test alongside eight other donor-conceived activists campaigning for access to their origins.

Of the 10, four turned out to share the same donor: Audrey, her brother Peter, Sophie and Sophie's brother David - highlighting how real the risk of a shared donor had always been.

Many years later, a genetic match with an American led Audrey to her donor - a man called Philippe - but he had already died.

Audrey's mother wrote Philippe's family a letter, thanking them for his "gift" which she described as "immeasurable".

His family welcomed Audrey for a visit. "Everybody had tears in their eyes," recalls Audrey. Philippe's sister had never known he was a donor.

The discovery gave Audrey answers that she had sought for decades. She learned details about her biological family's medical history. She saw photographs and video footage of Philippe. "I can watch him, see how he moved and hear his voice."

Audrey's legal campaign and Arthur's book together helped drive changes to French donor-conception laws, allowing people conceived after April 2025 to access identifying information about their donors when they reach adulthood.

For now, however, France remains one of the few countries in Europe where at-home DNA testing is still prohibited.

Which means, for Audrey, the wider fight continues.

"Every person has the right to know their origins and the right to know their history," she says.

articles.title: Why young Brits are going to Japan
articles.summary: Photos of Mount Fuji, bowls of ramen and the bustle of Shibuya Crossing are filling up social media feeds.
articles.body:
As I open up Instagram, I see another person in their late-20s has been to Japan.

It shouldn't come as a surprise any more.

"I cannot scroll through TikTok or Instagram without seeing videos of people in [convenience store] 7-11 and trying all the different skincare and trying all the snacks and the viral sandwiches and the viral drinks and going to all the viral restaurants," says Alex Baker, who has been to Japan three times.

There's been growing hype about Japan as a travel destination among young British people.

Data from the Japanese National Tourism Organization shows that 483,157 British tourists visited Japan in 2025, up 24.8% on 2024 and up 40.8% on 2019, the benchmark year used by travel companies to compare with pre-pandemic trends. Provisional data for 2026 suggests numbers are continuing to grow.

This reflects the boom in total tourism to Japan since the pandemic, with a record number of foreign visitors in 2025.

The Brits in their 20s and 30s I spoke to gave a long list of reasons for wanting to go to Japan - the cityscapes, food, anime, nature, history, gaming, temples. But they largely agreed that social media was the main driving force behind so many young people heading there.

When Maitri Sanghvi scrolled through TikTok, "Japan just kept popping up," she says.

It was a big reason why Maitri, 24, and her boyfriend went for three weeks earlier this year. "Seeing [Japan] on social media restarted my urge of wanting to go," she says.

Search #japantravel on TikTok or Instagram and you'll see countless videos of Mount Fuji, bowls of steaming ramen, itinerary suggestions, small villages in the Japanese Alps, the Fushimi Inari torii gates in Kyoto, the neon lights of Osaka's Dotonbori, and the chaos of Shibuya Crossing.

"Seeing other people's Japan videos definitely influenced my decision to go," says Aden Ibrahim, 29.

Since he went with friends last July, Aden has posted dozens of TikToks of his trip, and he's still uploading them more than a year later. One captioned "Japan made it out the group chat" has 1.1 million views.

Travelling to Japan isn't cheap - return off-peak flights with a layover in China start at about £450 with a budget airline. But the yen is weakening , making it cheaper for tourists when they're actually out there - even as rising prices hit residents. In July, the yen fell to a 40-year low.

"You can literally get a bowl of life-changing ramen for £3/£4 compared to a rubbish one here for like £20," says Faye Jawad, 26, who reviews restaurants on TikTok and visited Japan last year.

"When the yen was weakening, I thought 'actually this is a good time to go, things are going to be cheap'," says Vivek Haria, 26, who has a trip planned for this autumn. His interest in Japanese culture means he's wanted to visit for years - he has been learning the language and even sings in the UK-Japan Choir - but he says the value of the yen made it even more attractive.

The low prices have led to many tourists splashing out on souvenirs when they're out there. Videos of people showing off their Japan "haul" of flavoured KitKats, stationery and clothes have become popular on social media.

When Sam Corbett, 23, was in Japan in May he bought so many souvenirs - including snacks, matcha, clothes and skincare - that he had to buy an extra suitcase, which he stuffed full. Everything was "really affordable," he says.

Almost all the Brits I spoke to had stuck to the same route known as the Golden Route: Tokyo, Kyoto and Osaka, often with day trips to nearby destinations like Nara, Hiroshima and Mount Fuji.

It's easy to see why so many tourists pick this route. These cities are easy to travel between and packed with some of Japan's biggest attractions.

But complaints about badly-behaved tourists are sparking debate about overtourism.

Chiyuki Izumii, a tour guide for the Japan Guide Agency, feels tourist behaviour has got worse in recent years. She says that while her customers are respectful, she's seen other tourists jumping queues for buses, blocking space on board with big suitcases, carving their initials on trees in Kyoto's bamboo forest, speaking in loud voices at night and entering restricted areas to take pictures.

Some authorities are cracking down. Fujikawaguchiko, a town near Mount Fuji, cancelled this year's cherry blossom festival after repeated issues with misbehaving tourists, while Tokyo's Shibuya ward, home to the famous Shibuya Crossing, started issuing on-the-spot fines for littering in June.

In July, Japan increased its international tourist tax - typically incorporated into flight and boat tickets for people leaving Japan - from 1,000 yen (£4.60) to 3,000 yen, which it says will be spent on things like improving public transport and restoring historic sites.

Some visitors were surprised just how crowded major cities in Japan were.

"I was prepared for it to be busy but I didn't expect it to be as busy as it was," says Millie Dring, a huge anime fan who went in November with a friend to celebrate her 21st birthday.

The DisneySea theme park near Tokyo was so busy that Millie and her friend only went on one ride, which had a three-hour queue, and felt overwhelmed by the crowds.

Sam blames some of the crowds at tourist hotspots on social media hype and he says he regrets going to some places just because they were popular online. One dessert spot he went to in Kyoto after seeing it "all over social media" was very busy "and there wasn't a single local person in the queue," he says.

Sites like the Hakone torii gates and Arashiyama bamboo forest had huge crowds of people trying to get Instagram-perfect photos, he says.

But for some visitors, the hustle and bustle of the tourist destinations are all part of the attraction.

"I think there's a snobbiness around being a tourist over the past couple of years where people want to avoid looking like one," says Laura McGregor, 29, who's spending two weeks in Tokyo and Osaka in November for her honeymoon. Her plans include going to Disney and Universal, attending a sumo event, visiting Fuji and Hiroshima, and hiring go-karts to drive around Tokyo.

"Of course I want to experience an authentic side of Japan but I'm excited to embrace the tourist side too and go along with it," she says.

articles.title: Ukrainian nuclear power plant without external power for over a week
articles.summary: This is the 27th time since Russia invaded Ukraine that Zaporizhzhia plant has had to rely on emergency diesel supplies.
articles.body:
The Zaporizhzhia nuclear power station in southeastern Ukraine has been without off-site power for more than a week, the world’s nuclear energy watchdog has warned.

The plant, which Russia has occupied since 2022, is currently relying on emergency diesel generators, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) said on Saturday.

The plant needs power to keep its six non-operating reactors cool and has only a 10-day diesel supply on site, the IAEA said in a statement .

“The availability of diesel fuel is of paramount importance whenever a nuclear power plant loses off-site power,” IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi said.

The Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant has not had a delivery from an off-site storage facility in about six months but was supplied with diesel on Thursday and Friday from another off-site location, the IAEA said.

The Vienna-based agency is now trying to negotiate a local ceasefire to allow repairs to electrical lines.

Zaporizhzhia is Europe’s largest nuclear power plant. It has not generated electricity since September 2022, over six months after Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February that year, but the plant’s reactors must be kept cool to prevent a meltdown of the fuel inside.

“This is the 27th blackout at the plant since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion,” Ukraine’s deputy head of military law enforcement, Gyunduz Mamedov, wrote on X on Saturday.

The IAEA has had a permanent presence at the site since September 2022, after Russia took control of the Ukrainian facility in March that year.

Both sides in the conflict regularly accuse the other of attacking the site, which sits on the banks of the Dnipro River and demarcates the front line in the sector.

On Friday, the IAEA said there had been three incidents that week with drones at the plant, injuring two employees. It did not say who launched the drones.

Earlier this month, a drone strike close to the plant killed one nuclear specialist and wounded 17, with Moscow asserting that Kyiv was behind the attack.

Ukrainian officials have repeatedly warned that Russian actions in and around the plant constitute nuclear blackmail against Ukraine and Europe more widely.

In 2024, footage emerged of a fire in one of the power plant’s cooling towers, prompting Ukraine to accuse Russia of nuclear blackmail.

articles.title: Voting closes in Iceland’s knife-edge EU referendum
articles.summary: Iceland’s leadership has promised to honour whatever the country’s people decide.
articles.body:
Voting has closed in Iceland’s referendum on resuming membership negotiations with the European Union.

Voting stations closed on Saturday, but it could take several hours for a clear victory for either the “yes” or “no” camp to emerge.

The referendum does not have exit polls, and ballot counting only began once voting stations closed.

Polling suggests the vote is on a knife-edge , with different surveys putting either side narrowly ahead, but none straying more than a few points from an even 50/50 split.

The vote comes 13 years after Iceland, then led by a Eurosceptic government, paused EU accession talks.

The country is currently governed by the pro-EU Social Democratic Alliance, which called the vote and promised to honour whatever the Icelandic public decides.

If Icelanders vote “yes”, the country would likely start years of negotiations with Brussels to hammer out membership terms. It would then hold a second referendum on whether to formally become part of the EU.

Security, the relatively sluggish Icelandic economy, and the future of the Icelandic currency, the krona, have all been significant themes in the run-up to the vote.

articles.title: Trump-Putin-Zelenskyy summit floated in secret Moscow talks: Report
articles.summary: US News: CIA Director John Ratcliffe proposed a trilateral meeting between US President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President .
articles.body: CIA Director John Ratcliffe proposed a trilateral meeting between US President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky during his covert trip to Moscow this week, in a bid to revive efforts to end the Russia-Ukraine war, Axios reported, citing two people briefed on the matter.Ratcliffe's visit marked his first personal involvement in the Trump administration's diplomatic push to break the deadlock between Russia and Ukraine. He met Russian intelligence chiefs Sergey Naryshkin, head of the SVR foreign intelligence service, and FSB Director Alexander Bortnikov during his trip on Tuesday.According to the sources cited by Axios, Ratcliffe's talks partly focused on whether Russia's intelligence leadership could help persuade Putin to return to US-mediated negotiations with Ukraine.US officials briefed Zelenskyy on Friday about Ratcliffe's discussions in Moscow and the proposal for a three-way summit. The idea has been raised by the Trump administration previously, with Zelenskyy expressing support while Putin has rejected it.Ratcliffe seeks opening for talksRatcliffe also floated the possibility of restarting peace negotiations, according to the sources. The New York Times separately reported that he gave Bortnikov a bleak assessment of the war and pressed Russia to reach a deal before its position deteriorates further.The Axios sources said Ratcliffe viewed Bortnikov as a constructive interlocutor who could help restart diplomatic efforts. The CIA declined to comment on the discussions.The proposed summit comes as US-mediated negotiations between Moscow and Kyiv remain stalled. Talks were paused in mid-February after the war with Iran began, while White House envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have separately held discussions with Russian and Ukrainian negotiators in recent months without making significant progress.Ukrainian officials, however, remain deeply sceptical of Putin's intentions. Kyiv has said it has intelligence indicating that Russia could be preparing a major escalation.Zelenskyy's deputy chief of staff, Pavlo Palisa, said on Friday that Putin had ordered the Russian military to prepare several operational scenarios for an offensive in northern Ukraine, including around Kyiv and Chernihiv.At the same time, Zelenskyy's chief of staff Kyrylo Budanov said US-mediated talks with Russia could resume in September.Zelenskyy on Friday appeared to welcome Washington's latest diplomatic efforts, thanking the US for what he called the "necessary tone" of its conversations with Russia and saying the Trump administration was advancing a "realistic vision" of what needed to be achieved.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Canada installs large Lake Ontario sign in latest jab at US
articles.summary: Ontario Premier Doug Ford unveiled a billboard on Canada's shoreline with the message: "Lake Ontario. Now and Always."
articles.body:
Ontario Premier Doug Ford has hit back at Donald Trump by installing a large sign on Canada's shoreline with the message: "Lake Ontario. Now and Always."

The US president signed an executive order on Thursday seeking to change its name to Lake America and has shared a series of AI-generated videos about the lake that straddles both countries.

"Long before President Trump, this lake was called Lake Ontario. Long after President Trump is gone, it will still be called Lake Ontario," Ford said.

The war of words was triggered after trade talks collapsed, with the US imposing new 50% tariffs on $20bn (C$28bn) of Canadian goods. Canada will implement "dollar for dollar" counter-tariffs next month.

Trump said the decree was effective immediately as he signed the order to rename it Lake America.

While he has broad discretion over how the US recognises landmarks, other countries are not required to follow. Canadian officials have dismissed Trump's move.

On Saturday, Trump also posted several AI-generated videos on social media, with one showing him kicking over a Lake Ontario sign and replacing it with one that says: "Welcome to Lake America."

Another video depicted a flock of Canada geese sporting the US president's hair and holding rifles as they patrolled the shoreline of a newly named Lake America.

Ford said Trump's renaming of the lake was because he "didn't like Ontario and Canada standing up for ourselves".

Standing in front of the newly unveiled Lake Ontario sign, Ford added: "Just in case President Trump or anyone else forgets, we've set up this sign to remind them, it's Lake Ontario, now and forever."

It echoes Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney's previous response to the row, insisting "things must be called by their name, and this lake is called Lake Ontario - today and forever".

The names of four of the Great Lakes - Ontario, Huron, Michigan and Erie - originate from indigenous words. Lake Superior was named after an anglicised French word. Lake Ontario, the smallest of the Great Lakes, borders both the Canadian province and the US state of New York.

Trump's executive order gives the US Department of the Interior 30 days to update the name change with the Geographic Names Information Service - the official repository of domestic geographic names in the US.

When Trump entered the White House in 2025, he signed a similar order that changed the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America. Mexico has rejected the name change, arguing a single country cannot rename a shared body of international water.

It also led to a legal dispute between Mexico and tech giant Google, which renamed the gulf in its maps application.

In that case, Google Maps users in the US see "Gulf of America", while those in Mexico see the "Gulf of Mexico". Those in other countries see the "Gulf of Mexico (Gulf of America)".
